title: Adab with parents
hook: a man asks who most deserves his good company, and hears one answer three times

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of the market, and your line: easy in dealing. Did someone get a little more time from you? Today, the adab closest to home. Day one thousand three hundred one.

Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Then your father. Abu Hurayrah reports the exchange in Sahih al-Bukhari. A man had asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, which of all people most deserves his good companionship. He asked four times, and the answer didn't move until the fourth. Not a speech, not a list of virtues. One word, said again and again, until it couldn't be missed. Today's adab sits inside that repetition.
screen: `WHO MOST DESERVES MY COMPANY?` → `YOUR MOTHER. YOUR MOTHER. YOUR MOTHER.` → `THEN YOUR FATHER.`

segments.voice: Why say it three times? The hadith itself doesn't explain, but the Qur'an gives a picture. In surah Luqman, in Pickthall's translation: "His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness." The verse goes on to the weaning. The repetition sounds like a debt counted out loud. And the father isn't dropped. He's named, and his place is real. The question was about companionship, and the answer gives everyone a place in line. Then the Qur'an turns to how. In surah al-Isra, kindness to parents comes right after the command to worship none but Allah. When parents grow old, the verse says, don't even say uff to them, the smallest sound of irritation, the sigh before an eye roll. Pickthall renders the rest: "speak unto them a gracious word." And then the image of the wing: "lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy." A bird lowering its wing over its young. Here the grown child does it for the parent. And the verse gives a du'a to say: "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little." The adab has an honest edge too. Surah Luqman says that if parents push a child to associate partners with Allah, the child shouldn't obey, but should still keep company with them kindly in this world. Disagreement doesn't cancel kindness. So adab with parents isn't only obedience. It's company, a gracious word, a lowered wing, and a du'a. With the mother named three times.
screen: `WEAKNESS UPON WEAKNESS.` · `NOT EVEN A SIGH OF IRRITATION.` · `THE WING LOWERED THROUGH MERCY.` · `DISAGREE, AND STAY KIND.`

segments.voice: The practice: call your mother, or pray for her. Settle, and breathe. Bring your mother to mind, or whoever mothered you. Let her face arrive. If she's living and you can reach her, plan the call: when today, and one gracious word you'll say. If she has died, a hadith in Sahih Muslim counts a child who prays for a parent among the good that continues after death. If you pray, you can say the line from al-Isra: my Lord, have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little. If the relationship is hard, simply hold her in mind with whatever mercy is possible today. The bell holds the time.
Adab with parents. Good companionship, gentle speech and a lowered wing of mercy, with the mother named three times before the father. Today's word.
Your line: mother, three times. Today, call her, write to her, or remember her in a du'a, and your father too. Tomorrow, the adab with neighbors. Day one thousand three hundred one.

howItsDone: Muslims treat kindness to parents as a duty that follows worship of Allah, cite the hadith naming the mother three times, and recite "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little" for their parents, living or dead.
